title: Two Years of Change: A Reflective Account
paragraphs: I have been living in Uralsk for two years now. That sentence alone tells you something useful: I am still here, and the two years of living matter as a duration — as an experience I am still in the middle of, not one I have finished. If I said "I have lived in Uralsk for two years," it might imply — depending on context — that I've stopped. The continuous form keeps the door open.

In those two years, a great deal has changed. The city itself has not changed visibly — the same streets, the same markets, the same long winters. But I have changed. I have become more independent. I have developed routines that my previous self would not have recognised. I have learned to manage money in ways that my parents spent years trying to teach me. These are achievements — states that now exist because of what has been happening to me. They belong in the present perfect simple because they are complete in the sense that matters: they are real now.

At the same time, much has been happening that is not yet complete. I have been studying English for longer than any other subject. The study is not over — I am still learning, still noticing things, still surprised by what I don't yet know. I have been working on my thesis since October. The work continues. These things are in the present perfect continuous not because they are unimportant, but because they are alive — still in progress, still consuming my attention.

The distinction between the two forms maps onto something real about how we experience time. When something is finished, we step back from it and observe the result. When something is still in progress, we are still inside it — we can't step back yet. "I have read that book" creates a small distance: the reading is done, I am looking at it from outside. "I have been reading that book" puts me still inside the pages.

This is also why the present perfect continuous is so often used for explaining or excusing. "Sorry I'm late — I've been waiting for a bus that never came." "You look stressed — have you been sleeping properly?" "Why are your hands dirty? I've been fixing the car." The activity that has been happening explains the current state. The connection between process and present is the whole point.

What have I learned in two years that cannot be summarised in a list? I have learned that things take longer than you think they will. I have been discovering that the interesting problems are the ones that don't solve easily. I have become more comfortable with uncertainty. I have been getting better at staying in difficult things rather than leaving them when they get hard. These four sentences use simple and continuous almost interchangeably — yet each choice says something specific about how I experience the quality being described.
Two years. I have arrived, adjusted, struggled, grown. But I have also been arriving, adjusting, struggling, and growing — and perhaps I still am.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Your essay is brilliant. How long have you been working on it?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: About three weeks. But I've rewritten the introduction five times.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Or perfectionism. I've been struggling with the main argument. But I've finally written something I'm happy with.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I've been reading a lot about critical discourse analysis — and something clicked. I've applied the framework I've been reading about.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: I can see that. The essay reads differently from your previous work.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I've grown as a writer this semester. Slowly. But I have.

keyPhrases.context: "Still in progress." = not yet finished; ongoing.
"The distinction maps onto something real." = corresponds to; reflects accurately.
"'I have read' creates a small distance." = you step back from the completed thing.
"I have developed routines." = regular patterns of behaviour.
"Still consuming my attention." = taking up mental energy and focus.
"Used almost interchangeably." = can be substituted for one another.
"Adjusted to the city." = made changes to fit the new situation.
"Step back from it and observe the result." = create distance; take an outside view.

vocab.definition: a regular sequence of activities or behaviours
vocab.example: "I have developed routines my previous self would not have recognised."

vocab.definition: in a way that each can replace the other
vocab.example: "Simple and continuous used almost interchangeably — yet each choice says something specific."

vocab.definition: to devote time and effort to something
vocab.example: "Five rewrites! That's dedication." — sustained committed effort.

vocab.definition: a structure or system for approaching a problem
vocab.example: "I've applied the framework I've been reading about." — analytical approach from study.

vocab.definition: written or spoken communication in extended form; a field of study
vocab.example: "Critical discourse analysis." — the study of how language shapes and reflects power.
"The city has not changed visibly." — not in ways that can be observed.

vocab.definition: to suggest something without stating it directly
vocab.example: "'I have lived' might imply — depending on context — that I've stopped."

vocab.definition: the state of being unsure or not knowing
vocab.example: "I have become more comfortable with uncertainty." — a result of two years' growth.

task1Items.question: "I have been living in Uralsk for two years" — ___ form keeps the door open.
"I have become more independent" uses PPS because the change is now ___ .
The writer has been working on their thesis since ___ .
"I have been reading" puts the reader ___ the pages — still involved.
"Sorry I'm late — I've been waiting for a bus." PPC ___ the current state.
Kamila has been ___ about critical discourse analysis.
The writer has developed ___ their previous self would not have recognised.
The last paragraph shows both forms: "I have arrived" and "I have also been ___ ."

task2Items.statement: "I have been living" implies the speaker has finished living in Uralsk.
"I have become more independent" is PPS because the change is a completed state.
"I have read that book" puts the speaker still inside the reading process.
PPC is often used to explain a present visible state.
The text says the thesis work was completed in October.
Kamila has rewritten the introduction five times.
The text says PPS and PPC can never be used almost interchangeably.
"I have grown as a writer" describes a completed achievement — a result.

questions.text: Why does the writer use "I have been living" rather than "I have lived"?
opts: "Have been living" keeps the door open — they are still living there
Both mean exactly the same thing
questions.correct: "Have been living" keeps the door open — they are still living there
questions.hint: "The continuous form keeps the door open." — still here, still in the middle of it. ✅

questions.text: Why does the writer use PPS for "I have become more independent"?
opts: The change is now complete — the state exists in the present
questions.correct: The change is now complete — the state exists in the present
questions.hint: "They are complete in the sense that matters: they are real now." — PPS for completed states. ✅

questions.text: What image does the text use to distinguish "I have read" from "I have been reading"?
opts: "Have read" = outside the book (done); "have been reading" = still inside the pages
questions.correct: "Have read" = outside the book (done); "have been reading" = still inside the pages
questions.hint: "'I have read' creates distance: the reading is done, I am looking from outside. 'I have been reading' puts me still inside the pages." ✅

questions.text: Why is PPC used in "Sorry I'm late — I've been waiting for a bus"?
opts: PPC explains the current state (lateness) through past ongoing activity
questions.correct: PPC explains the current state (lateness) through past ongoing activity
questions.hint: "The activity that has been happening explains the current state." ✅

questions.text: "I have been getting better at staying in difficult things rather than ___ them when they get hard."
questions.hint: "...rather than LEAVING them when they get hard." — PPC describes the ongoing improvement process. ✅

questions.text: What does the final paragraph mean by "I have arrived... but I have also been arriving"?
opts: Arrived = completed event; been arriving = the ongoing process of adapting is still in progress
questions.correct: Arrived = completed event; been arriving = the ongoing process of adapting is still in progress
questions.hint: PPS = the completed event (arrival). PPC = the ongoing process of settling in, adapting, still in progress. ✅

opts: A system or structure for approaching a problem
questions.correct: A system or structure for approaching a problem

opts: The studying is ongoing — not yet complete; still in progress
questions.correct: The studying is ongoing — not yet complete; still in progress
questions.hint: PPC for ongoing process that's still happening. "Still learning, still noticing things." ✅

questions.text: "I have grown as a writer." vs "I have been growing." — the difference?
opts: "Have grown" = completed achievement; "have been growing" = still growing, in process
questions.correct: "Have grown" = completed achievement; "have been growing" = still growing, in process
questions.hint: PPS = achievement (grown — I am now more developed). PPC = still in process (still growing). ✅
